idiom_name: POSIX message queue per type (mq_open("/orders")) + per-queue decoder table
implementation_notes: The closest thing to a channel in the C toolbox is a named POSIX message queue: one queue name per message type (/orders, /invoices) is the type binding, and each receiver opens exactly the queues it serves, so the type comes from the name it opened and never from a tag inside the payload. Nothing in the compiler protects that binding, so materialize it as data - a table mapping queue name to decode/validate function - otherwise senders and receivers drift apart silently and a mis-sent message is only noticed when the receiver misreads the bytes. Remember that queue attributes are per queue: mq_msgsize and mq_maxmsg are set at mq_open time (with kernel ceilings in /proc/sys/fs/mqueue), so a queue per type means several deliberately dimensioned queues, and POSIX queues persist in the kernel until mq_unlink. Where the transport is a broker instead (MQTT topic, AMQP routing key, ZeroMQ prefix), the same rule applies with the topic string as the channel identity.
pitfalls: Queue limits are per queue and small by default (mq_msgsize 8192 bytes, msg_max 10 messages): a message larger than the queue's mq_msgsize is rejected with EMSGSIZE, and N types means N small buffers instead of one deep one.

POSIX message queues are local to one host and persist until mq_unlink: a queue per type multiplies the cleanup obligation, and the descriptors are only pollable/selectable on Linux, which the portable code path cannot assume.
The compiler never checks that /orders carries only orders: a sender writing a different struct to the same name is accepted by the kernel and only shows up as garbage in the receiver.
